draft.title: Transforming exponential graphs
card: For \(a > 1\), the graph of \(y = a^{x}\) passes through \((0, 1)\) and rises from left to right. The x-axis is an asymptote: the curve gets close to it but never touches it.
Adding \(k\) gives \(y = a^{x} + k\). Every point moves up by \(k\) units, or down if \(k\) is negative. The asymptote moves from \(y = 0\) to \(y = k\).
The y-intercept moves too. Put \(x = 0\) into \(y = a^{x} + k\) and you get \(y = 1 + k\).
Example: \(y = 2^{x} - 3\) has asymptote \(y = -3\). Its y-intercept is \(1 - 3 = -2\), so it passes through \((0, -2)\).

1.alt: The curve \(y = 2^{x}\), rising from left to right, passing through the point \((0, 1)\) and getting closer to the x-axis on the left.

4.alt: The original curve \(y = 2^{x}\) dashed and the curve \(y = 2^{x} - 3\) solid, shifted down 3 units, with horizontal asymptote \(y = -3\) and y-intercept \((0, -2)\).

draft.remember: Adding \(k\) to \(y = a^{x}\) moves the whole graph and its asymptote to \(y = k\).

a.why: Adding 2 moves the graph up 2 units, so the asymptote moves from \(y = 0\) to \(y = 2\). The option \(y = -2\) has the direction of the shift reversed.
a.clue: The asymptote moves by the same amount as the graph.

b.q: Mia sketches \(y = 5^{x} - 4\). Where does her graph cross the y-axis?
b.why: Put \(x = 0\) in: \(5^{0} - 4 = 1 - 4 = -3\). The point \((0, -4)\) is tempting, but it is the asymptote level, which the curve never reaches.
